collection.description: You'll be taking the left-hand path, the traveler says pleasantly, before a villager has said a word.

ask.text:
(Name) is heading out on a long errand when (he/she) reaches the place where three paths divide. There, leaning on a staff wrapped in faded red cord, stands a traveler in a plain cloak that smells of salt, though the sea is half a day away.
"You'll be taking the left-hand path," the traveler says pleasantly, before (name) has said a word. That's exactly the path (name) meant to take. (Name) hasn't told a soul. The traveler just smiles, waiting, as if this happens every day. What should (name) do?

c1o1.text: "Take the middle path," the traveler says. "Cross at the shallows. Not the bridge." (Name) does as (he/she) is told, grumbling about the longer walk. On the way home, (he/she) passes the end of the usual route and sees the old rope bridge hanging in tatters over the brown, rushing river, torn loose sometime that morning. (Name) sits down on a rock for a while before walking on.

c1o2.text: "Go right," the traveler says, with a twinkle. "You'll want a bigger basket." The right-hand path winds down into a hidden valley where the mango trees are so heavy with fruit their branches touch the ground. (Name) has to make three trips to carry it all home. When (he/she) goes back to thank the traveler, the crossroads is empty. Your villagers gain (award) food.

c1.text: "Well, since you seem to know where I'm going," (name) says slowly, "is there a better way?" The traveler taps the staff thoughtfully against a stone...

c2o1.text: The traveler gives a name. (Name) knows it. It's the name of a villager who died many, many years ago, a name on an old grave at the edge of the village. "That can't be," (name) whispers. The traveler only smiles and walks off down the right-hand path. (Name) checks the grave that evening. It's still there, mossy and quiet, and that's somehow worse.

c2o2.text: The traveler laughs and gives a perfectly ordinary name. "I trade salt between the coastal villages. Half the people on this island take the left path to reach the river, you know. Lucky guess." (Name) feels a bit silly. They chat about the price of salt for a while, and then go their separate ways.

c2.text: "Who are you?" (name) asks. "How do you know where I'm going?" The traveler bows...

c3o1.text: They swap stories for miles. The traveler is funny and kind and knows every bird by its call. At a bend in the road, the traveler says, "This is where I leave you," and steps around the corner. (Name) follows a moment later. The road behind the bend is soft, wet mud, smooth and unmarked. There's no one there, and not a single footprint.

c3o2.text: By the end of the walk, the traveler has asked (name) a hundred questions about the village: the huts, the farms, the research, the children. "It sounds like a good place," the traveler says. "Do you think they'd have me?" They would. The traveler moves into the village that same week, and nobody ever does find out how (he/she) knew which path (name) would take.

c3.text: "If we're going the same way, we may as well walk together," (name) says. The traveler seems pleased, and they set off side by side...

c4o1.text: The right-hand path is a bit longer and a bit muddier, but (name) gets where (he/she) is going and back without trouble. (He/She) never sees the traveler again. Nobody else in the village ever did see (him/her).

c4o2.text: The right-hand path splits, and splits again, and soon (name) has no idea where (he/she) is. (He/She) wanders in circles all night, tripping over roots and scraping (his/her) shins, and finally limps back into the village at dawn, exhausted, scratched and soaking wet. "Should have taken the left," someone says. (Name) does not find this funny.

c4.text: (Name) doesn't like being predicted. Just to be stubborn, (he/she) turns on (his/her) heel and takes the right-hand path instead...
